methodological_rigor.justification: This is a large nationwide Swedish registry cohort of 778,943 women with vaccination treated as a time-varying exposure, delayed entry by attained age, linkage to vaccination, patient, cancer, population, death, education, and income registers, and exclusions for pre-entry vaccination or lesions. The design is well matched to vaccine effectiveness and population-program questions, with adjustment for age, calendar year, county, maternal birth country, parental education, household income, and parental HPV-related disease history. Statistical methods are appropriate, using Poisson regression with IRRs and 95% CIs, time-varying age and calendar year splitting, and sensitivity analyses with 1- and 2-year buffer periods plus site-specific vulvar and vaginal analyses. Remaining limitations include observational residual confounding from unavailable smoking and sexual behavior data, possible vaccination and outcome misclassification, no randomized allocation, and limited separate cancer analysis because of few cancer cases.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study is an individual population-based cohort study, corresponding to Oxford level 2b. The clinical and public-health relevance is direct because HPV vaccination is a modifiable prevention strategy and high-grade vulvovaginal lesions and related cancers are clinically meaningful HPV-associated outcomes. The observed adjusted reduction among vaccinated women, especially those vaccinated at ages 10 to 16 years, and the lower incidence in subsidized and catch-up cohorts support earlier and broader vaccination programs. The evidence is not practice-changing on its own because causal interpretation is limited by residual confounding and registry misclassification, but it strongly informs prevention policy.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the appropriate standard and the manuscript explicitly states adherence while reporting population source, inclusion and exclusion criteria, registry linkages, exposure and outcome definitions, covariates, follow-up, statistical models, sensitivity analyses, and key limitations. The results provide cohort size, vaccination counts, follow-up, event counts, IRRs with 95% CIs, and birth-cohort program comparisons. Reporting is strong, although table contents and supplement details are not fully visible in the normalized text and there is no explicit public data or analytic code availability statement. Reproducibility is limited by reliance on linked national registry data and proprietary SAS/Stata analyses without shared code in the manuscript.

novelty_literature.justification: The study extends established HPV vaccine effectiveness evidence from cervical lesions to rarer high-grade vulvar and vaginal lesions using nationwide registry data. The introduction notes that only one observational Danish study had assessed similar high-grade vulvar and vaginal outcomes, so the Swedish population-based replication and program-level birth-cohort comparison are meaningful empirical additions. The concept is not first-in-class because HPV vaccination protection against HPV-related noncervical lesions is biologically and clinically expected and supported by prior trials and observational data. Novelty is therefore moderate rather than high.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly organized with a structured abstract, explicit research question, detailed methods, and results that consistently report absolute rates, adjusted IRRs, confidence intervals, and sensitivity analyses. The discussion links the findings to prior trial and Danish observational evidence and gives a balanced limitations section covering misclassification, screening differences, HPV status, residual confounding, and causal interpretation. Figure captions are informative, especially the cumulative incidence caption explaining time-varying exposure handling. The writing is concise and publication-ready, with only minor dependence on supplemental tables for full detail.

key_strengths: Very large nationwide cohort with individual-level linkage across vaccination, cancer, patient, population, death, socioeconomic, and family-history registers.
Vaccination is modeled as a time-varying exposure with age as the time scale and calendar-time adjustment.
Sensitivity analyses with buffer periods and separate vulvar and vaginal lesion analyses support the main association.
The study addresses a clinically important but less well-studied HPV-associated prevention endpoint.
key_concerns: Residual confounding from unavailable smoking, sexual activity, and health-seeking behavior remains possible.
Vaccination status and vulvovaginal lesion ascertainment may be misclassified in registry data.
Vulvovaginal cancers could not be evaluated separately because of limited cancer cases.
No explicit public data or code availability is provided in the normalized manuscript.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a strong population-based vaccine effectiveness study with direct preventive relevance and careful registry methods. It is appropriate for a high tier-2 oncology or public-health venue after minor clarification of reproducibility, missingness, and residual confounding.
